en: The Telakaṭāha Gāthā Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One. May the Lord of Laṅkā,
who walks with the gait of a king of elephants, be victorious!
With arms long, thick, and beautiful like the coils of the lord of serpents,
devoted to noble conduct, an abode of virtues,
established in the Dhamma, and free from anger, pride, and arrogance;
He who is honored by the entire world, whose dwelling is compassion,
the source of liberation, a full moon in the sky of the solar dynasty,
has fully awakened to the vast ocean of all that is to be known.
Bow your heads in homage to that Lord of Sages, supreme in the world;
he is the stainless flight of stairs to the abode of the Thirty-Three,
a bridge for crossing over the ocean of saṃsāra.
Always revere the Dhamma proclaimed by the Sage— the secure path free from the fear of all states of existence—
and whatever is worthy of being given, however small, with a mind full of faith.
Having given, people obtain a fruit far more excellent;
therefore, always pay homage to the Saṅgha, which is praised by the One of Ten Powers and is a field of merit for those seeking peace.
By the great power of the Triple Gem,
one attains liberation throughout the three worlds;
there is no protection equal to that of the Triple Gem.
Therefore, O sirs, always venerate that Triple Gem: the Lord of Laṅkā,
who delights in the welfare of others, is free from desire,
ever rejoices in wakefulness even at night, and is the abode of compassion.
He awakens the world for the benefit of the world; therefore,
practice the Dhamma according to your desire, devoted to wakefulness,
intent on helping beings, and having virtuous companions.
O people, rare on this earth are those who have overcome negligence;
having found as a companion in virtue the Lord of Laṅkā, whose wealth is his qualities,
practice the stainless Dhamma and abandon negligence.
The Dhamma is the supreme refuge for the three worlds, the highest among all flavors;
the Dhamma is the most precious jewel among jewels in the world;
the Dhamma is the cause for destroying the suffering of the three realms of existence.
Practice the Dhamma, devoted to wakefulness;
dispel sleep and cultivate the immeasurable.
Contemplate here the suffering, the impermanence, and the non-selfhood [of all things].
Abandon attachment to the body, which is like a decaying vessel;
practice the Dhamma, devoted to wakefulness.
There is no time for me today; I shall do it tomorrow.
Thus, for those who delight in the application of skillful means here in this world,
there is no liberation from death for a human being, even if they were to rule over the three worlds or the entire triple universe.
Just as a clod of earth thrown by anyone into the sky reaches the ground in an instant through its own momentum, so too, in this case,
the very fact of being born is indeed the sole cause.
Indeed, the world is always destined to go toward death;
for a man falling from the summit of a mountain,
there is certainly nothing in mid-fall that can serve as a cause for escape from fear.
Sentient beings in the three realms of existence may indeed go toward death;
therefore, abandon delight in wealth and even in life itself.
Indeed, torrents of rain fall down upon the earth.
Just as a flash of lightning is released from the mouth of a spreading cloud,
so do men fall at will into the midst of the terrifying abyss of death;
indeed, there is no one constant among the realms of existence.
Just as the rows of waves on the shore of the ocean,
the abode of waters, never cease to come and go,
so too do men and gods never cease to pass away.
Though surrounded by fierce beings in the ocean of death—
with chariot chiefs, lordly elephants,
and warriors with their forces and weapons— [he was not afraid].
Having always transcended the world, that bull among men destroys desire as one strikes down a stalk of grain in the three worlds; O,
like a lamp extinguished by a great wind, [he is unshaken].
Even that which is of great splendor quickly meets with destruction;
likewise, in this world, the great lamp of human life is swiftly extinguished by the fierce wind of death.
And kings such as Rāma and Ajjunappa, preeminent among men,
who were heroes victorious over hosts of enemies at the front of battle in their cities—
even they have here had their bodies submerged in the flood of fierce death.
Who in this world has not passed away, who is liberated from death? Fortune,
the ocean-clad earth with its mountains,
various prosperities, and even the beauty of form— none of these remain.
All those friends, sons, and wives, and whoever else—
do they follow anyone who is departing toward death? Even the Brahmās, Asuras,
and hosts of Asuras of great power [cannot].
The gandhabbas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and rakkhasas— all these and others alike fall at the end into the crest of the fire of death, like moths whose merit is exhausted.
And those disciples of the Sage headed by Sāriputta—
pure, always free from taints, and having attained supreme success—
even they have been swallowed up in the jaws of the snare of Death.
Just as lamps are destroyed by fire and reach their end,
so too are the Buddhas— those whose beautiful eyes are like stainless lotuses,
whose physical splendor is adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
The Protectors of the World, who bring about the destruction of all fetters,
have been thoroughly trampled by the great elephant of death;
they feel compassion for those afflicted by disease, but not for those afflicted by old age.
Death, like a great lordly elephant,
constantly slays the world— even those delicate youths devoted to play—
just as a forest fire consumes an entire grove without exception.
Neither the fullness of the water nor the abundance of the reservoir satisfies the firewood,
nor does the quantity of fuel satisfy the consumer;
even if he were to consume the entire three worlds without remainder, he would remain unsated.
O, Death is indeed merciless and finds no satisfaction!
O, through delusion and being bewildered,
the helpless and wretched world falls even into the most terrifying mouth of Death.
One of inferior wisdom finds delight in sensual pleasures,
which are as unstable as a swing or a wave and comparable to a dream;
yet even a single person is capable of striking down the three worlds with death.
Why are even those who are merciless pursued by old age and death?
Or what man, once born, would place his hope for life in things that are as fleeting as beautiful dreams?
Having seen this world as perpetually afflicted, full of fear and sorrow, and overcome by anger, intoxication, delusion, and old age—
if there is not even a trace of agitation in one who perceives this, [then he is truly wise].
Alas, that death is indeed so terrible! Fie upon it!
O sirs, do you not see Death, who carries the sword of old age, constantly slaughtering the entire three worlds?
Why do you lead [lives] so pitiless and devoid of fear?
Practice the Dhamma, which always dispels the darkness, with heedfulness.
O friends, cultivate it for the sake of avoiding death and Māra.
For that self-controlled man who always maintains this perception of death in the world and delights in such cultivation,
craving residing within his body is abandoned without remainder.
Aging makes even the most beloved form grow foul;
a terrible disease robs one of all strength,
leaving the body unprotected from various misfortunes.
O Death, what fruit is there in destroying this physical existence?
Those who have perished at the mouth of the vast ocean of saṃsāra— where the waves of disease are driven by the winds of karma— are truly ruined.
Do not be heedless; strive for liberation!
For men, the arising of suffering is indeed rooted in heedlessness;
so too are wealth, friends, children, servants, and kinsmen.
Even one's wife, who is as dear as life itself,
and all one's fields and property— none of these follow one departing from this world to the next,
just as neither merit nor demerit in the world follows one.
O friends, cast as you were into the ocean of existence by that great storm of past karma,
the ship of the body will surely be shattered in an instant, flickering like lightning.
Take hold of the supreme essence of virtue with your hands;
for in this world, the selfhood, though guarded in many ways, constantly breaks apart like an unbaked clay vessel.
Practice the Dhamma, which is the foundation for reaching heaven;
the Dhamma, when well-practiced, yields fruit even in this very life.
Having rejoiced eternally in the celestial kingdom of the gods, which is more delightful than anything else—
Even the wise gods fall when their merit is exhausted;
all happiness, whether in heaven or on earth, ends in separation.
What person of wisdom would take delight in the pleasures of existence?
The Buddha, the sole protector of the world together with his assembly of disciples,
is like the full moon surrounded by a garland of stars;
even Indra, whose lotus-feet are adorned by the crowns of the gods.
Who among those born within the three realms of existence has not been like a mass of foam?
Even the beauty of youth’s form, which is like a playful crest-ornament,
and union with beloved people— though they seem comparable to oneself— are likewise fleeting.
Even having seen [this world] as flickering as lightning,
O people deluded by ignorance and stained by passion for existence, you still practice negligence;
a son becomes a father, and here a husband becomes a son.
A woman may at one time be a mother, a father, and a son;
thus the world of the living constantly revolves,
for the stage of birth is indeed ever-fickle in its nature within the mind.
Even the gods, having sported in the past in the Nandana grove with celestial beauties amidst various flowering creepers,
once found themselves in places crowded with widely spread thorns.

Alas! Even those who were the foremost of gods in the celestial cities of heaven, having enjoyed exquisite food from golden vessels and attained supreme prosperity, now suffer pain in the Koṭisimbalī forests.
And they, having come to dwell in the abode of hell,
will at times even swallow glowing iron balls;
whereas those supreme lords of men have enjoyed the entire earth without exception.
The lords of the gods enjoy the most delightful celestial bliss in heaven,
while at other times they dwell upon the earth covered with hooves;
or those hosts of great chariot-warriors follow them here in the sky.
In that city, where the rows of waves were gracefully broken,
which was followed by the crest-jewels in the matted locks of the Lord of the Earth,
the excellent gods sported together with their celestial consorts.
And they fall into the most terrible Vetaraṇī river;
whereas [others enjoy] the delightful and enchanting Nandana groves, abounding in blossoms, sprouts, creepers, and fruits.
Even the peaks of Kailāsa and Meru,
with their mouths like full caves made lovely by celestial nymphs, go to destruction;
for sensual enjoyments are indeed like the wind, fire, and waves upon a swing.
Life is as flickering as the flash of lightning,
and the body is like an illusion, a mirage, or the moon reflected in water;
who would feel attachment to life or to worldly prosperity?
What suffering exists that is not found within these dreadful states of existence?
What being is not a vessel for that manifold suffering, being born as one overwhelmed by death, disease, and old age?
What wise person would crave the delight in existence, like a fool?
Or who would swallow a glowing iron ball,
even if it could somehow be grasped with the palm of the hand?
Who indeed, unless they be a fool, would desire this body, which is the source of suffering, a flow of impurities, and endless? In this world,
there is no fear for human beings equal to that of death.
There is no suffering equal to the suffering of disease,
nor is there anything like old age in its power to deform;
yet, O people, one still finds pleasure in the body through delusion.
Because of himself, he ruins himself— like a plantain tree, a reed,
or a banana tree that perishes from its own fruit;
even when supported, like an ungrateful companion who betrays his benefactor.
The body, which resembles a lump of foam, is like a thorn of poison;
it is the abode of water, wind, fire, earth, and serpents,
and time does not follow after him who has transcended it.
Seeing his own physical being utterly frail like a decaying house,
how could a wise person find delight when the exhaustion of life approaches moment by moment?
Death follows, with old age as its staff, to slay;
time does not turn back that which has passed.
Is this suffering in the realms of existence not indeed inconceivable?
For those of short life, death is easily encountered within the realms of existence;
for those of long life, there is aging and manifold calamities.
Thus, in the realms of existence, there is only suffering from both sides.
Practice the Dhamma for the destruction of suffering;
for those dwelling within the prison of existence throughout the three worlds,
who are tormented by the great fire of suffering.
For all eternity there is no time for negligence in well-conducted conduct, O sirs! Accumulate the supreme wholesome.
Pleasure is but slight, like a drop of water on the tip of a blade of grass, O sirs!
Suffering indeed pervades the entire world like the waters of the ocean;
for even the mental formations are by their very nature suffering,
and thus the whole of the three worlds is nothing but suffering alone.
The body does not follow him for the sake of the body;
the fool undergoes manifold suffering here in this world,
for the body is always a stain, a mire, and a defilement.
One who delights incessantly in the body goes to ruin; for it is a maker of filth,
a source of the impurity of the Kali age, a stench of raw flesh,
and a locus of spears, swords, arrows, venomous serpents, and diseases.
Behold this body, the abode of old age and death—
empty, ever devoid of essence, and deserving of reproach; alas,
this selfhood is suffering, impermanent, and impure!
Do not bring about defilement; never indeed does anything permanent exist.
O friend, for even the slightest thing lacks essence;
practice the essential Dharma and avoid negligence.
In these five aggregates and six sense-bases, which are like an illusion, a mirage, the core of a plantain tree, a mass of foam, and the waves, water, and bubbles of the Ganges;
Since no self exists at all, what fool would not say so?
Yet one might run for a much longer time, holding on to a yoke, with a chariot made of a barren woman’s son and the horns of a hare.
One might say that the body is even weaker than a lamp’s final flicker, which perishes in an instant;
just as a fool [might value] a vessel made of water-bubbles.
One might indeed drink the water of a mirage to one's throat,
or out of delusion speak of this selfless body as being substantial, like a plantain tree devoid of core.
The fool who desires to clothe himself with the flower of the udumbara tree or with the water of a mirage meets only with distress;
he ruins himself for his own sake.
The self is never found here in this body;
for just as one who thoroughly peels apart a plantain tree would not find even the slightest core, so it is with the person.
Within the five aggregates and those six sense-bases,
which are all empty, one would not find even the slightest essence;
apart from the threads, there is no such thing here as the state of a cloth.
Indeed, there is no being whatsoever that exists apart from the body;
the body itself is devoid of intrinsic nature and subject to momentary dissolution.
Who else on this earth exists for the sake of the self?
For just as a foolish deer, seeing the water of a mirage from afar, runs toward it perceiving it as real water,
so too [does one run] toward that which is devoid of intrinsic nature and established through perversion.
For one conceives passion for the body through such conceptualization;
yet in the body, which is devoid of intrinsic nature and established only by conceptualization,
no self exists, just as there is no lightning in the sky.
Devoted to meditation and free from negligence,
cultivate the perception of non-self in order to destroy all taints—
[this body] which is smeared with saliva, mucus, blood, tears, and fat.
Beings always avoid this body, which is defiled by the impurities of the kalpa, devoid of essence, and loathsome,
just as one would avoid a jar filled with various kinds of filth.
For even if a person were to bathe in all the waters of the four oceans and possess a fragrance as great as Mount Meru, that scent would be unsurpassed;
yet such a person never attains true purity.
"O sir, what quality do you perceive? What is there in this physical form?
This very body is a repository for various impurities;
this very body is the locus of slaughter, bondage, and disease."
That very body, with its nine apertures split open,
is a terrifying cemetery even without a corpse,
for it contains within itself the elements of urine and excrement.
Once one has departed from the body and passed beyond it,
even mother and father would become pitiless and their love destroyed;
how much more so, then, would this be true for kinsmen, children, and wives?
This body, with its nine openings, is a dwelling for swarms of worms;
it is a foul-smelling mass of flesh, sinews, bones, and blood—
those who nourish it by practicing various evils here [are truly pitiable].
Truly, how deluded they are regarding this body,
which is subject to death, like a water bubble, a dwelling place for various diseases,
and always filled with blood, urine, and excrement!
The man who delights here in these things that are like food for a moon-wolf will surely grieve in the next world, for he is of childish intellect; indeed,
O friend, he is like a mass of foam, devoid of essence.
Always emitting a foul odor like a pit of filth,
resembling the abode of venomous serpents, full of fear and suffering,
this body constantly flows like a broken jar of salt water.
Just as a lotus born upon the earth is not to be censured even when it arises from mud and turbid waters,
so too is the welfare of others, though it takes form within the body.
That [body] is never at all blameworthy here in the world;
for it is far superior to the bodies of the hosts of men and women in the world by more than a thirty-second part.
What fruit is there here for the wise regarding their bodies?
Surely it is that very thing which is service to others;
nevertheless, the body of even a more learned person [is used] in that same way.
One’s own self should be protected for a much longer time;
indeed, if one lives for a very long time, one should practice the Dhamma.
For the Dhamma is truly like a supreme jewel that grants all desires.
Just as the potency of a medicinal herb,
when well-processed within milk, becomes manifest through its affinity with the milk,
so too does the Dhamma, when practiced here in the world, become manifest.
Just as a shadow follows one departing for the next world from this one,
so too does a shadow appear beautiful upon a polished, stainless mirror, according to the form fashioned by the body.
Having likewise performed the highest wholesome deed for the sake of the future life,
they become as if adorned by that very fruit; even so,
within the body which is a dwelling place for manifold sufferings.
Under the sway of delusion and negligence,
bewildered by the perception of pleasure, the one of inferior wisdom—
like one licking honey from the edge of a sharp razor— experiences intense suffering.
The one of little wisdom who has not abandoned the passion of intention,
whose being is devoted to that [passion], always encounters suffering;
for the deluded one, there is the perception of happiness in this world of sense-pleasures.
Indeed, when examined closely, it is like the kiṃpākaphala;
though you possess all enjoyments and the acquisition of various wealth and grain,
O sir, you are like one whose form resembles the makara-bannered god [Kāma].
That man who, even in his youth, meets death against his will—
having been one who took the wealth and the lives of others at will—
becomes a beggar with a broken alms-bowl in his hand.
Shaven-headed, reproving him with hundreds of harsh words,
he lived in a poor man’s dwelling clad in tattered rags—
a man who, though his body was elsewhere, stole the hearts of others.
A woman never truly escapes from the state of being a woman;
even if she were a man in another life, he who commits adultery with another's wife, which is not to be transgressed, will always become a woman again.
He always encounters terrible and manifold calamities;
he becomes wretched, foul-faced, dull-witted, and witless;
he is perpetually mute and unpleasant to behold.
For that person of little wisdom who speaks false speech, having become a human being, he attains incomparable suffering;
they become like madmen, devoid of shame and virtue.
Always wretched and devoted to calamity and sorrow,
they are born with deformed bodies in various states of existence;
having drunk the surā liquor like the halāhala poison, they have lost their wisdom.
By whomsoever evil deeds were committed here in this world,
even for many countless millions of years,
having obtained terrible and incomparable suffering in the hells—
And herein one encounters manifold and numerous calamities;
for there is nothing in all the three worlds that brings peace to the world like the Triple Gem.
By that very great splendor, may I, having conquered all evil, always attain all happiness;
and may all beings throughout the entirety of the three worlds likewise do so.
May friends, enemies, and kinsmen— all of them—
always be free from disease and fear, free from sorrow,
and having attained every happiness, may they be joyful.
The body is like a broken jar filled with dung;
the body is always an abode of impurity, foulness, and calamity;
and the world suffers for the sake of all pleasure within the body.
The body is always the abode of death,
disease, and old age; it regards beings neither as "young," nor as "old," nor as "children," but is merely tormented by death.
Thus, whether standing, lying down, or departing,
I am inevitably going to the mouth of Death;
for such is this body, possessed of its inherent defects.
Always keep that in mind within your hearts:
cultivate loving-kindness, the protection of the foul, and mindfulness of death;
being devoted to meditation, remain constantly self-controlled.
Having performed meritorious deeds such as giving, which have happiness as their fruit, and having measured out that entire result here,
one should always give for the welfare and happiness of others.
What indeed is that essence which has truly come into one's hand?
For nothing whatsoever exists in the world without a cause;
even sound is born from the cause of striking the palm.
And thus the world, distinguished by the differentiation of the states of cause and fruit, arises, perishes, and persists;
for it is composed of the causes of karma, just as ignorance is.
O friend, through karma one attains the distinctions of birth;
and depending upon birth, beings constantly experience the suffering of aging,
death, and so forth, throughout beginningless time.
Just as there is no more karma here through the destruction of delusion, so too, with the exhaustion of karma,
there is no birth in the realms of existence; and with the exhaustion of birth,
the suffering of old age, death, and so forth ceases here.
"Like an island consumed by fire through the wind,
he who here constantly beholds the Dhamma-body of the Sage—
the Buddha— he is the man who truly sees," so he said.
O friends, seek out the Buddha, the stainless Dhamma, and the Protector of the Three Worlds,
and likewise investigate the nature of phenomena;
for it is like a well-sharpened arrow plunged into the heart.
Cast away this triad of defilements, smeared with the stains of various evils,
a vessel for manifold misfortunes, and devoid of faith,
by means of the hook made of wisdom.
And all the worldly conditions do not shake his mind,
which is forever free from the thorns of evil defilements,
even when confronted by the various sense objects such as forms, all gathered together.
Just as Mount Meru’s peak is shaken by a great wind,
so too the Lord of Sages, having crossed the ocean of the profound perfections,
cannot reckon the suffering of saṃsāra.
The subtle truth has been realized by him whose net of delusion is destroyed;
therefore, always strive for the supreme benefit of others,
having abandoned even the bliss of liberation you yourself have attained.
I wandered through existences full of great terrors for the sake of others' welfare;
thus, always placing the benefit of others before me,
I have practiced the Dhamma solely for the sake of the world.
Having obtained this human birth, which is most difficult to find,
and having attained the perfection of opportunity free from all conceptual proliferation,
and having understood the Dhamma that leads to the destruction of the taints and is for one's sole benefit—
What wise person would not devote themselves to the unsurpassed Dhamma,
having obtained the Buddha’s teaching— which is exceedingly rare,
the peerless Path of the True Dhamma, and likewise the bestower of peace?
What wise person would not cultivate the supreme Dharma, which brings about the excellence of wisdom through association with the most excellent spiritual friends? Even so,
it is exceedingly difficult to find when one has obtained such a favorable existence.
Free from the fault of stinginess, desiring the welfare of both worlds,
endowed with the qualities of faith and the rest, and always heedful—
O, O, perform merit for the attainment of the Deathless!
